title: rustler_precompiled distribution for ash_vault_rustler
description:
The NIF package currently builds from source, so every consumer needs a Rust toolchain — this repo's own host has cargo but no linker, which is exactly the situation to design for.

Specced step by step in ash_vault_rustler/README.md and deliberately not wired: a base_url pointing at a nonexistent release turns every mix test into a NIF load failure. Needs a real release first.
notes:
PREP DONE - ISSUE STAYS OPEN. Cannot be completed without published release artifacts.

Done (all of it compiles and tests green on both branches):
  * ash_vault_rustler/mix.exs: added {:rustler_precompiled, "~> 0.8"} alongside rustler. NOT optional: - the "use" in AshVaultRustler.Native is chosen at COMPILE time, so whichever the switch picks must already be present. Also added a package/0 that ships checksum-*.exs, and the alias "mix nif.checksum" -> rustler_precompiled.download AshVaultRustler.Native --all --print.
  * ash_vault_rustler/lib/ash_vault_rustler/native.ex: both "use" forms behind a switch. @precompiled_by_default is false, so an ordinary build is unchanged - plain "use Rustler". ASH_VAULT_RUSTLER_PRECOMPILED=1 takes the RustlerPrecompiled branch; ASH_VAULT_RUSTLER_BUILD=1 forces a source build on it (what CI uses). Target list and base_url live here. Verified BOTH paths compile clean with --warnings-as-errors, and the default path still passes the whole suite.
  * .github/workflows/nif-release.yml (new; .github did not exist): 6-target matrix via philss/rustler-precompiled-action, on a "ash_vault_rustler-v*" tag or workflow_dispatch, attaching artifacts to the release.
  * ash_vault_rustler/README.md: the old aspirational section replaced with what is wired, how to exercise it locally, and a 6-step "Releasing a precompiled NIF" checklist for the maintainer.
  * ash_vault_rustler/test/precompiled_switch_test.exs (3 tests): asserts the default build is still from source with a message pointing at the checklist, that the checksum file is absent, and that every target in Native.targets/0 is actually built by the workflow - so the two copies of the target list cannot drift.

WHAT REMAINS (needs a real release, in this order):
  1. Confirm base_url names the real repo. It is currently https://github.com/jakeschurch/ash_vault/releases/download/ash_vault_rustler-v#{@version} - a moved or renamed repo silently 404s here.
  2. Push tag ash_vault_rustler-v<version> and get every matrix job green. A missing target is a hard compile error for consumers on it, not a soft failure.
  3. Run "mix nif.checksum" and COMMIT checksum-Elixir.AshVaultRustler.Native.exs. Without it in the package, RustlerPrecompiled refuses a downloaded artifact.
  4. Flip @precompiled_by_default to true in AshVaultRustler.Native, and update precompiled_switch_test.exs (it is the tripwire that fails first if 4 happens before 2 and 3).
  5. Verify from a clean checkout on a machine with no Rust toolchain that mix deps.get && mix compile succeeds. That is the entire point and the one check that cannot be done in the repo that produced the artifacts.

The workflow itself is unverified - it has never run, since running it means cutting a release.
close_reason:
Released ash_vault_rustler-v0.1.0 with all six targets. Verified from a clean clone on a machine with no linker: mix compile pulled the precompiled artifact and the full 158-test suite passed.

Three things went wrong and are worth recording:

1. philss/rustler-precompiled-action installs cross unconditionally (aarch64-apple-darwin failed identically with use-cross: false) and that install is broken — giantswarm/install-binary-action, tar exit 1. Bumping v1.1.4 -> v1.1.5 changed nothing. Replaced with a direct cargo build; cross is not needed now that ubuntu-24.04-arm runners exist.

2. musl links the CRT statically by default, which suppresses the cdylib entirely. cargo succeeded and produced no .so, failing in packaging rather than the build. Fixed with -C target-feature=-crt-static.

3. nif_versions was not declared, so RustlerPrecompiled asked for 2.15 artifacts CI never built and mix nif.checksum 404'd. Now pinned to 2.16, which covers OTP 24+.

title: unique? is effectively Postgres-only
description:
The transformer generates an identity for unique?: true but sets no pre_check_with. On any data layer without native identity support (ETS, and others), Ash.DataLayer.Verifiers.RequirePreCheckWith raises at compile time: 'The data layer does not support native checking of identities.'

Reproduced while validating an audit finding. Either set pre_check_with, or reject unique?: true at compile time on such data layers with a clear message naming the limitation, rather than letting Ash's generic error surface.
close_reason:
Chose rejection + explicit opt-in over silently setting pre_check_with.

Implemented in lib/ash_vault/transformers/setup_encryption.ex (verify_uniqueness_enforceable!/2) plus a new encrypt option pre_check_with: in lib/ash_vault/dsl.ex.

Evidence for the choice: pre_check_with DOES work on ETS — the pre-check before_action hook runs after AshVault.Changes.Encrypt, so email_lookup is populated when the check queries for it, and a duplicate is rejected through normalization. Probed directly. So this was a cost decision, not a correctness one. It is a full read action on every write (deps/ash/lib/ash/changeset/changeset.ex:3261-3330) and it is not race-free. Adding a query per write on the user's behalf to make a DSL option compile is not a trade to make silently.

Option 2 alone would have left no fix, so the error names an option the user can actually set:

    encrypt :email, searchable?: true, unique?: true, pre_check_with: MyApp.Domain

Detection: data layers lacking native identity enforcement declare Ash.DataLayer.Verifiers.RequirePreCheckWith in verifiers/0 (ETS: deps/ash/lib/ash/data_layer/ets/ets.ex:49; Mnesia: mnesia.ex:42). Postgres does not, so the generated identity there still carries pre_check_with: nil and costs nothing.

Tests: test/ash_vault/unique_on_ets_test.exs (7) — the option lands on the identity, duplicates rejected including via :downcase_trim, nils never conflict, the DSL error names the option and is not Ash's generic message, searchable?-only still compiles on ETS, and Postgres has no pre_check_with. Docs: documentation/topics/searchable-fields.md, unique? section.

title: OpenBaoTransit provider: never export the DEK
description:
A KeyProvider that does encrypt/decrypt inside OpenBao rather than exporting key material, so the raw DEK never enters the BEAM. The genuinely strong answer to key material in process memory, at the cost of a network round trip per value.

Requires a KeyProvider contract that returns no raw key — the AshVault.Key opaque handle added for the Rust NIF is the seam. See documentation/topics/threat-model.md and docs/QUEUED_WORK.md.

Deferred repeatedly because it changes the provider contract while other work was in those files.
notes: Docs corrected after review: cost is THREE round trips per value (measured with a [:finch,:request,:stop] counter, asserted in test), not one; exporting provider is 3 encrypt / 2 decrypt and drops to 0 behind Cached, while Cached does nothing for handles (is_binary/1 guard). Delta: +57 tests mine (35 provider, 20 cipher/e2e, 2 runtime outage).

title: Document the two erl_crash.dump findings as a recurring hazard
description:
Two 11-12MB erl_crash.dump files appeared during this project (repo root and example/), one referencing the key provider modules. A crash dump is process memory on disk, outside every protection the library provides.

documentation/topics/operations.md now covers ERL_CRASH_DUMP_SECONDS=0 and ulimit -c 0, and both files are gitignored. Open question: should the library itself warn at boot if crash dumps are enabled in prod? Cheap to check, and this happened twice in one project.
close_reason:
Decided IN FAVOUR of a boot warning, and implemented.

First, the fact the decision hinged on, verified empirically rather than from memory (OTP 29, this nix shell): with ERL_CRASH_DUMP_SECONDS unset, erl writes erl_crash.dump on abnormal termination; with it set to 0, nothing is written. So the unsafe state is the DEFAULT.

Why warn, despite a library warning about host configuration being presumptuous:
  1. The unsafe state is the default, and the hazard is process memory on disk - decrypted plaintext plus key material for any provider holding it on the BEAM heap, including scopes already crypto-erased. That is outside every protection this library offers.
  2. It happened twice while building this library, in a project whose whole subject is key hygiene.
  3. One environment variable; the fix is one line.

What keeps it from being noise - all three are tested:
  * Fires ONLY when the variable is unset. Setting it to anything, 0 or 30 alike, is a decision and is respected in silence. The warning is about the absence of a decision, never about the answer. This is the main defence against presumption.
  * Fires ONLY in :prod, via a compile-time-captured Mix.env() - and the whole branch is compiled out elsewhere with an "if @env == :prod", not checked at runtime, because a runtime check leaves a provably-unreachable branch that fails --warnings-as-errors in dependent projects.
  * Fires once at boot and is suppressible: config :ash_vault, warn_on_crash_dumps?: false
  * The message carries the fix (ERL_CRASH_DUMP_SECONDS=0), the alternative, "ulimit -c 0", and the off switch.

Deliberately NOT done: no ulimit -c check. Reading the limit is not portable, and a warning right about one half of the hazard and silent about the other teaches the wrong lesson. The message says so explicitly, and operations.md covers both.

Code: lib/ash_vault/application.ex - crash_dump_warning/3 is a pure function so the decision is testable without booting under another Mix.env.
Test: test/ash_vault/application_test.exs, 9 tests - when it fires, that it says what to do, and the three restraints, including that it logs nothing in :test.
Docs: documentation/topics/operations.md gained "AshVault warns about this at boot" with the reasoning and the suppression switch; the two-dump history is now recorded accurately (both files, both sizes).
Smoke-tested for real: MIX_ENV=prod mix run --no-start emits the warning; the default mix test run does not.

title: evict_scope/1 erpc multicall path is uncovered
description:
ash_vault_rustler: evict_scope/1's :erpc.multicall/5 never executes in the suite because Node.list(:connected) is empty on one node. The decision it feeds is well covered — classify_evictions/2 is public and unit-tested against every :erpc shape — but the four lines wiring multicall to it are not.

Matters because this is the path that makes cluster-wide erasure synchronous: a node that does not acknowledge must fail the destroy.
close_reason:
Covered for real with peer nodes — :peer.start_link/1 works in the nix dev shell (OTP 29), so no substitution was needed.

New: ash_vault_rustler/test/cluster_eviction_peer_test.exs (9 tests, async: false, @moduletag :cluster which is NOT excluded by default) and ash_vault_rustler/test/support/evict_stub.ex.

Approach: :net_kernel.start/1 with a randomized longname, then real peers. Each peer gets only AshVaultRustler.Test.EvictStub, pushed over with :code.get_object_code/1 + :code.load_binary/3 — not the whole application, because the property under test is the fan-out, not the cache, and a peer that could not load the NIF would fail for an unrelated reason. The stub reads its answer from the peer's own :persistent_term, so one peer acknowledges while another refuses. Cached.evict_scope/2 is called with a hand-built opts map pointing :backend at the stub.

Covered: the multicall actually running (asserts both peers are in Node.list(:connected) first, so the file cannot pass by skipping the branch it claims to cover); a peer answering {:error, reason}, named and isolated from the healthy peer; a peer that cannot run the call at all (stub never loaded -> :undef); a peer that does not answer in time (timeout); a peer killed mid-flight; a peer whose call raises; cluster: false not fanning out. Plus two destroy/2 tests: a non-acknowledging node yields {:error, {:cache_evict_failed, {:nodes_failed, _}}}, and full acknowledgement is what permits :ok.

Gotcha worth recording: a :peer node has the Erlang kernel but no Elixir stdlib, so the stub must use :erlang.error/1 and :timer.sleep/1 — Process.sleep/1 and raise/1 come back as :undef from RuntimeError/Process and the test asserts the wrong :erpc shape.

Mild flakiness risk: the 'vanishes mid-flight' test relies on a 200ms sleep landing inside the multicall window. Passed on every run so far.

ash_vault_rustler suite: 146 -> 155 with this file.

title: OpenBao lookup key name injectivity is accidental
description:
lookup_key_name/1 is key_name(scope) <> '_lookup'. The audit proved it cannot collide with key_name/1 for any scope, but only by an accident of base64url alphabet arithmetic — a canonical unpadded base64url string ending in '_lookup' would need an impossible length or specific low bits in 'p'.

A collision would mean one tenant's lookup key IS another tenant's data key. Make the property deliberate: a comment explaining why, and a property test asserting it.
close_reason:
Audit confirmed independently, no collision possible — NOT a P0. Verified two ways: the arithmetic by hand, and by brute force over every canonical unpadded base64url string ending in '_lookup' at total lengths 7, 8, 9 and 10.

The proof, now in lookup_key_name/1's moduledoc: a collision needs enc(s1) == enc(s2) <> '_lookup'. Writing n = byte_size(enc(s2)), enc(s1) has length n+7, and n is never 1 mod 4.
  n=0 mod 4 -> n+7=3 mod 4: final char of a 3-char group must have low 2 bits zero; ?p is index 41, 41 &&& 3 == 1.
  n=2 mod 4 -> n+7=1 mod 4: not a legal unpadded base64 length.
  n=3 mod 4 -> n+7=2 mod 4: final char of a 2-char group must have low 4 bits zero; 41 &&& 15 == 9.

Sharper than the original audit: the remaining residue n+7=0 mod 4 needs n=1, and canonical strings ending in '_lookup' DO exist at length 8 — 'A_lookup' is Base.url_encode64(<<3,249,104,162,75,169>>, padding: false). All 64 of them are excluded by the length rule alone, not by ?p. Both halves of the argument are load-bearing; the moduledoc and a test now say so.

Test: test/ash_vault/key_providers/open_bao_key_name_test.exs, 11 tests (5 StreamData properties), untagged so it runs in a plain mix test. The discriminating assertion is the single-scope form 'key_name(scope) never ends with _lookup' — the pairwise form the issue suggested passes vacuously, since two random scopes never collide. Also: exhaustive over every scope of 0-2 bytes; the suffix pinned to what lookup_key_name/1 actually appends; the alphabet index of ?p; and that the encoding is unpadded. That last one matters most — with padding: true a collision IS reachable, so it is the assertion standing between this and a real bug.

title: Lookup.field_key/3 bypasses Runtime.resolve_scope!/3
description:
lib/ash_vault/lookup.ex:277 calls scope.resolve!/1 directly rather than going through Runtime.resolve_scope!/3, so a custom AshVault.Scope returning a non-binary escapes as a raw ArgumentError from a provider's validate_scope!, instead of the InvalidScope error the runtime raises everywhere else.

Loud, not silent — but it is a wrong-shaped error escaping a non-bang Ash.read/2. Found by the silent-failure audit, ranked below its two main findings.
close_reason:
Fixed. Lookup.field_key/3 now calls AshVault.Vault.Runtime.resolve_scope!/3 (made public, signature changed from (ctx, opts, operation) to (ctx, scope_module, operation) so callers pass opts.scope rather than a fake opts map) with operation :lookup. A non-binary scope now surfaces as AshVault.Errors.InvalidScope naming the scope MODULE, instead of a bare ArgumentError naming whichever key provider's validate_scope!/1 saw the term first. field_key/3's existing rescue already listed InvalidScope, so a non-bang path now gets {:error, %InvalidScope{}} where it previously got a raw raise.

Regression test: test/ash_vault/searchable_fields_test.exs, describe 'a scope that is not a binary (ashvault-8i0)' (3 tests), backed by a new resource AshVault.Test.EtsNonBinaryScopeDoc in test/support/resources.ex whose vault is NonBinaryScopeVault. Verified to fail without the fix with exactly the old symptom: '(ArgumentError) AshVault.KeyProviders.Memory scopes must be binaries, got: {:tenant, "acme"}'.

Not done, deliberately: AshVault.Errors.MissingScope's verb/1 has no :lookup clause, so a MissingScope raised on this path still renders as 'Cannot encrypt'. errors.ex is owned by another agent this session; not a regression (that path never set an operation before).
